title: Chapter 28 – Congratulations in Advance
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The voice settles over Green Pine Hill like warm water.

"Brother Lin! I have come a long way, and in a hurry, and I hope you will forgive the dust. Word reached me that this is a good day for your house. I thought: a neighbor should be at the gate."

Lin Jian does not breathe. Through the slit in the hut wall he can see the whole yard, and nobody in it moves. Even the horses at the bottom of the hill have gone quiet, as horses do when a thing larger than they are walks past.

```
[Scan — Zhao Heng (distance 200 paces, passive)]
Cultivation: Foundation Establishment, late stage
Qi density: 9.3× Qi Refining peak
Shell: continuous, radius ~12 paces, not a talisman, not a spell
Artifact: jade ring, right hand — Profound grade (Defense class)
Full structural read: BLOCKED at this range / interface level
CE: +5 (total: 142 / 400)
```

Nine point three. A man at Foundation Establishment does not carry his Qi, he wears it, thick and smooth and gently glowing, the way a heavy cloak is worn.

The telemetry hums at the edge of his sight.

```
Subject: Lin Zhenshan — Stage 2
Compression: 77%
Pulse 71
Backlash risk: moderate → elevated (external pressure detected)
Ring integrity: 100%
```

He can feel it too. A cold shadow has fallen over the hill, and in the chamber a man with his whole life crushed into the size of a fist has noticed.

"Zhao Heng." The answer comes from the east wall. It is not carried on any thread of Qi. Father simply stands there in his gray cloak and says it, in the clear, plain voice he uses for reading letters aloud. "You are not expected."

"I am a neighbor, Wenyuan. A neighbor is not expected. That is rather the point of one." Zhao Heng chuckles. "Your steward was kind enough to light a candle for us this morning. A small one, on the north ridge. It saved me the trouble of guessing the hour."

The third beacon. Lin Jian shuts his eyes for one breath. Wenhai's.

"My steward," says Father, "is in your custody."

"Your uncle is a lonely man with a gift for arithmetic. He is my guest." Zhao Heng's tone is perfectly kind. "I carry a petition from him, in fact, written in his own hand, asking that if the worst should befall your father today, a neighbor of standing should come and keep order. You know the clause. It is a very old clause. It is very wise. It was written for days like this."

"My father is alive."

"Then I rejoice. And since he is alive, and so busy, I will not disturb him." The voice warms still further. "I will simply stand here, outside your gate, with my escort, and wait. A neighbor is entitled to stand at a gate. The Compact says so, and the Enforcement Hall, I think, would say so more strongly. If he rises from his chamber a Foundation Establishment cultivator, I will be the first to bow. And if not..."

He leaves it. It hangs there, light and sweet, like the smell of an overripe peach.

Lin Jian opens his eyes.

The riders have fanned across the road. Thirty and some: twenty-four in gray-green cloaks with the ridge-and-sun badge, and behind them, on rough horses, three who are not wearing badges at all. A gaunt woman in a dust-colored cloak. A big man with a coil of black chain across his shoulder. A narrow figure in a long gray cloak, standing very still. And Zhao Qian, on a tall bay, with a saber across his saddle bow.

Neighbors don't bring hired men. But the Compact makes room for that too. Hired men are not Zhao men. A Zhao man who killed a Lin in cold blood would be hauled before the Hall. A stranger who happens to be hunting a thief on the same road is merely unlucky.

He doesn't need to attack. He needs someone to break the ring. Anyone.

"Go home, Uncle Zhao," says Father.

"Wenyuan..."

"I know the clause, and I know the Compact." Father's voice does not rise at all. "And I know what a candle on a ridge is for. Go home."

Zhao Heng laughs, once, softly, like a man who has been told a good joke at a funeral, and lowers his hand.

"Qian," he says. "Escort the gentlemen to the gate."

* * *

They do not run. That is what is frightening. The twenty-four come up the road at a steady walk, in a block four across and six deep, with round shields locked on their left arms and the slips for Iron-Skin pasted to their chests. Behind them walks Zhao Qian, with his saber on his shoulder. The three hired killers drift out to the flanks like hounds.

The village guards have Silent Spears. The cousins on the tower have fifty slips in their hands, and seven days of Mother's drills have made them very good with them.

"Now," says Mao.

Six Flame-Burst slips leave the gate tower, bright orange, twisting like leaves. They strike the front of the shield block at once. Six bursts of red flame, loud as dropped doors, and the block stops dead for one breath, with a stink of scorched pepper. A shield goes up in a spray of sparks. A man is thrown back into the one behind him. But the Iron-Skin holds. They close the gap and come on.

Lin Jian watches the block's feet.

They are walking in a curious, careful rhythm, the whole block shifting a little left and a little right, in a pattern that does not match the road at all. He has seen that pattern on a map. He drew it.

They are walking between the pins.

Wenhai's map. Wenhai, who walked every stone of the old road at his father's heels, must have drawn the nine locations on a scrap of paper in the Zhao study. The block steps around each pin-stone by a pace. They have been rehearsing.

```
[Formation Key :: Road net]
Pins: 9 (idle)
Block position: nodes 3, 5, 7 within 2 paces
Net shape available: fold (concave), clamp (lateral), pit (vertical)
Load: 0 / each
```

They know the stones. Lin Jian's thumb finds the edge of the bronze disk. They don't know the shape.

A pin is a point. A net is a surface. Any pin on its own would throw a spike of force into the earth, easily avoided by a man who knows where to step. But nine pins, linked through the key, do not throw spikes. They throw a field, and the field fills the whole region between them, and in that field, by his own design, the earth is not a wall at all. It is a sheet of cloth.

Fold, he thinks. And pulls.

It takes no more than a breath. The road between the pins sinks, as if a giant hand had pressed a thumb into dough. A pit opens under the front of the shield block, shallow, not more than waist deep, but wide as a barn floor. The first rank goes in with a shout. The second rank, shields locked, cannot stop. Then the third. Dust boils up. Twenty-four men and their shields pile into the hollow in a roaring heap, Iron-Skin and all, while above them the earth that was the road folds shut again, gently, like a hand closing, and traps their legs to the knee.

From the wall, a single cry goes up. The village guards, thirty men with Silent Spears, are over the parapet and down on the pit in three heartbeats. They are farmers. They have been told only one thing: Spears at the knees, not at the faces. They do exactly as they are told. Mortal steel on armored shins, and an Iron-Skin slip lasts three breaths and not four.

"Fold!" Mao is roaring, delighted. "Brother Wenyuan, that's my nephew!"

On the road, Zhao Qian has not stopped.

* * *

He comes through the gate on foot, with the saber out and his head a little down, as a man walks into rain. He has jumped the pit in a single step. The yard dust lifts around his boots. He is a handsome man in good clothes with a cold, still face, and the air around his saber blurs, a thin shimmering arc of bright Qi that spreads in a quarter circle before him like a rising sun.

Silent Horizon Domain. The Qi along the blade does not cut. It erases. Anything inside the arc simply stops being there.

Old Hu steps into the gateway.

He has not moved from his place. He has not spoken. He stands in a leather apron with his rod across his shoulders and his iron lid on his left arm, a short, thick, stooped figure under a wall of noon light, and Zhao Qian reaches him and cuts.

The arc hits the lid. There is a sound like a drumhead splitting. Sparks fly in a bright, ugly fan. Hu does not step back. He does not step forward. The rod comes down off his shoulders in a short flat swing, and the saber bends to meet it and the two weapons ring together like a bell struck once.

"You're slow," says Old Hu.

Qian cuts again.

It is not a fight any of the watchers could follow: two men three feet apart, and the air between them shaking. Qian is faster and stronger. Hu has the lid and the rod, a thousand hours at the anvil, and a skin that is slowly turning into something other than skin. Every cut that lands leaves a bright scar on the iron and a new tear in his sleeve. He is bleeding in four places. He does not seem to notice.

He is holding him. In a gate too narrow for two, it is enough.

Beyond them, the others come in.

The woman first, floating over the wall as a dry leaf floats, in a cloud of dust. The gaunt woman in the dust-colored cloak: twenty paces off the ground, with her arms crossed and her sleeves belling out, and around her, thin and bright as glass, a spinning shell of wind. She comes down on the east wall. She smiles. She opens one hand, and a sheet of air tears the parapet in half.

Father meets her at the edge.

He has one slip in his left hand and the old sword in his right, and the sword is shaking, a ripple now instead of a rattle.

She is QR8. He is QR3. The numbers fall into place. He cannot win this.

She cuts. Father vanishes.

It is Cloudstep: two paces, left, no faster than thought. The air-blade goes through the place where he was. He reappears with his sword up and cuts upward, a plain clean arc, and the wind shell flares and swallows it. She laughs. She flicks her wrist, and he is thrown back against the stone, and slides.

And as the woman steps forward to finish the man she thinks is helpless, Lin Jian notices something he should have noticed before.

The shell is breathing.

```
[Scan — Gaunt woman, wind shell]
Type: Infinite Horizon Art (air blade cycle)
Shell integrity: 100 → 100 → 100 → 31 → 100
Recast interval: 6 breaths
Weak point: shell reforms from the crown downward; during recast, left shoulder open (0.4 s)
CE: +4 (total: 146 / 400)
```

Six breaths. He counts. One. Two. Three. Four. Five.

On the tower, a small figure with a Tidal Spear stands at the end of a row of cousins, not moving, not blinking. She has not fired once. She waits as a cat waits at a hole.

One of the eighteen nail plates is set under the planking at Mother's feet. They worked out a code in the forge, the two of them, without ever quite saying so: one tap means now.

Six.

He taps.

A single short pulse down the key, one tap, no stronger than the touch of a fingertip. Through the net, through the nail, up the post and the planking into the sole of a woman's boot.

On the tower, Su Qinghe's eyes do not move. But her wrist turns, a hair.

The Needle leaves the Tidal Spear as a pale hairline thread, so thin that the sun cannot find it, and goes eighty paces across the yard in a single breath. The wind shell is a bright sphere, a perfect glass bubble, with one small hole in it the width of a rice grain, open for four-tenths of a second at the crown of the left shoulder. The Needle goes through the hole as a stitch goes through cloth.

The woman stops. She looks down. A line of red is spreading from her left collarbone down her arm.

Then her shell collapses in a ring of dust, and she falls, and Father steps forward off the wall and puts the point of his sword at her throat.

"Alive," he says, to nobody. "Take her alive."

Lin Jian lets out his breath.

On the tower, Mother lowers the Tidal Spear and does not look at the hut.

* * *

It is the narrow man who does it.

He has been so still that Lin Jian has half forgotten him: a thin, pale, stooped figure in a long gray hood by the south corner of the wall. As the woman falls, he unfolds his hands, takes a black slip from his sleeve and slaps it against his own chest.

He is gone.

It is not Cloudstep. It is a shadow talisman of some high grade, the sort that costs more than the whole Lin treasury. A flickering gray streak slides along the base of the wall, a line of shade that moves where no shade should, across the packed earth and round the granary, past Feng and his runners, who turn and shout and throw. A Flame-Burst bursts on empty stones.

He's not going to the gate. He's not going for the wall.

The line of shade slides straight toward the stone hut.

Poison. Of course. He remembers the paper twist and its ninety-four percent. A man who works in powders does not need to cross a ring to ruin a ceremony. One breath of the wrong dust through the keyhole is enough.

Forty paces from the ring. Thirty. The twelve pins sing under Lin Jian's thumb.

Think. The ring will hold a late Foundation cultivator for a quarter of an hour. A Qi Refining eighth is an insect to it. Then I do not need all of it.

```
[Formation Key :: Ring net]
Pins: 12 (idle)
Target: Qi Refining 8 (hostile), approach vector 187°, 22 paces
Suggested: triangle bind (pins 4, 7, 11), hold duration ≈ 4 heartbeats
Cost: 3 pins (burn-out on release)
```

A triangle is the smallest shape that holds a thing in place. It will cost him three pins, and a ring of nine is a weaker ring than a ring of twelve. He has run this arithmetic in his sleep for a week.

Four heartbeats. And someone has to be watching.

He pulls.

The three pins rise out of the ground with a sound like cloth tearing. Blue light snaps between them in a pure, perfect triangle, and in the middle of the triangle, at a dead run, a thin gray man in a long hood comes to a stop with one foot in the air.

He does not fall. The triangle has taken him by the shadow, the bones and every muscle at once, and he hangs there, a wasp in amber, with his black slip burning down to ash in his hand.

One.

On the tower, Mother's head comes up.

Two.

She puts her hand into her sleeve. She takes something out, small and bright, between two fingers. It catches the light.

Lin Jian's heart stops.

It is a pin.

A little iron pin an inch and a half long, so true that even across eighty paces the sunlight runs along it like water along a wire. He knows it. He tuned a Fabrication run to ninety-nine percent to make it, and left it in a notch of a blood-spiral basin in a cave behind a frozen waterfall. He never thought he would see it again.

She took it. The knowledge arrives in one long cold sweep. She went back to the cave. She cleaned my footprints. She kept it.

Three.

Su Qinghe sets the pin to the Tidal Spear.

It is not what anyone is taught. The Needle is a thread of water, and a thread of water carries nothing. But a pin made perfectly, with a head that fits the throat of the spear, is a lance that needs no flight. She narrows the shaping seal until her fingers touch, and the Needle takes the pin on its back, and the water around it freezes to a hair of ice.

An eye. A joint. The hole in a shield. It is what she told him at the frozen river.

Four.

The pin leaves the spear with no sound at all.

It crosses the yard in a streak of pale silver and goes through the narrow man's hood just above the left eye, and out of the back of his head, and into the wall of the granary behind him in a puff of brick dust. The man's head snaps back. His whole body goes slack in the triangle, and then the heartbeats are over and the blue light dies and he drops, as a puppet does when the strings are cut.

On the tower, Mother takes one step back and goes down on one knee. The Tidal Spear clatters to the planks. A cousin catches her arm. She shakes him off, gently, and sits with her head bowed, breathing hard, and does not look up.

```
[Formation Key :: Ring net]
Pins: 9 of 12
Burn-out: pins 4, 7, 11 (cores cracked)
Ring integrity: 71%
```

Seventy-one. The number is a stone in his mouth.

* * *

In the road, the village guards have finished with the pit. It is not quite a rout, more thirty farmers methodically prodding twenty-four armored men until the last throws down his shield.

At the gate, Hu and Zhao Qian are still locked in their ringing dance. And on the wall above them, Feng sees his chance.

He has not been told to. He has been waiting at the head of the stair with his eight runners, and he has watched his aunt kill a man at eighty paces and the guards bury a Zhao block in a hole. He has the practice sword at his hip, a Fever-Cooling in one sleeve and a Sound Mirage in the other.

He draws the sword, and goes over the parapet like a falling leaf.

Lin Jian sees a shape dropping, light and quick, and Qian's head turning toward a sound.

"Hu, you old fraud!" shouts Lin Feng's voice, from the left, off the parapet, high and breaking and perfectly clear. "Let the boy through!"

Sound Mirage. Qian's blade swings left, toward the voice. The arc lights up the place where no one stands, and in the same instant the true Feng drops out of the air on the right, two paces behind the saber, with his sword in a low, flat, two-handed grip.

He does not cut at the man.

He cuts at the light.

Crescent Edge. A bright thin curve of Qi along a plain steel blade. And the steel, hardened in a forge by a refiner who did not ask questions and quenched in a way that no one on Green Pine had ever seen, does something that no practice sword should be able to do. It goes through the arc. It goes through the bright shell of the Solar Wheel as a knife goes through a dried gourd, and it bites into the wrist behind it.

Zhao Qian screams.

It is a short, shocked sound. The saber falls. The arc dies. He staggers back, clutching a right hand that hangs from the end of his forearm at an angle no hand should hang, and his face, for the first time, is no longer cold. It is the face of a man who has just been beaten by a child.

"Wrist," says Hu, with great satisfaction, and puts his rod across the man's chest and pushes him out into the road.

Feng stands in the gateway, panting, with the sword shaking in both hands. He stares at it. His eyes are huge.

"That was the book," says Lin Jian, under his breath, to nobody. And smiles, a little, and does not know why his eyes sting.

In the yard, the chain man has come over the south wall with his black chain whirling, and Mao steps down from the tower to meet him. The chain, an Azure relic that smothers fire and water, strikes the Earth Rampart Mao throws up and rings off it like a bell. It does not smother stone. Mao grins, a wide slow terrible grin, puts his shoulder into the wall, and the wall comes forward.

That one will hold for a while.

Zhao Qian is on his knees in the road with his arm held to his chest, and four guards are dragging him away. The air is thick with smoke, pepper and dust.

And Zhao Heng has dismounted.

* * *

He comes up the road alone, on foot, at a leisurely stroll, with his hands clasped behind his back and the sun flashing on the jade ring.

He is not hurrying. He steps around the pit as one steps around a puddle. He passes his fallen guards without a glance. When one of the cousins on the tower, a boy of sixteen with white knuckles, throws a Flame-Burst at him, the slip tumbles twice through the air and stops.

It stops a foot in front of Heng's face and hangs there, glowing, humming faintly, an orange flower in the air. Then it falls to the dust and goes out. Another slip, and another. Six in all, thrown from the tower in a desperate fan. They freeze, one after another, at the edge of an invisible line twelve paces from his body, as if they had struck a pane of glass.

He glances at them. Then up at the tower, and nods, kindly, to the boy.

"Very good," says Zhao Heng. "Pepper-ink. An old Lin recipe. Your grandfather would be proud."

Lin Feng steps into the gateway.

He does not say anything. He does not shout. His practice sword is still up, with a smear of Qian's blood on the edge, and he has sheathed neither his anger nor his terror. He lifts the blade to his shoulder and walks toward the Foundation cultivator like a boy walking into surf.

"Triple root," says Zhao Heng, looking at him with real interest. "Gu Yan was right about you. What a waste."

He lifts one finger.

It is not a blow. There is no sound. Feng goes backward as if a horse had kicked him, twenty feet, thirty, his sword spinning out of his hand, and strikes the wall of the gatehouse with a sound like a dropped sack, and slides to the ground, and does not move.

"Feng!" Mao's roar. Father's voice, a long way off, saying the same word.

"Peace," says Zhao Heng. "He is only winded."

Old Hu steps in front of him.

He has put the broken lid down. His rod is across his chest, in both hands, and his old padded cloak hangs in strips from his shoulders. His face is gray under the soot. There is an expression on it Lin Jian has never seen: neither anger nor fear. Something like a man who has come to the end of a very long road, and has found the person he was going to meet.

"Not past me," says Hu.

"Refiner." Zhao Heng sighs. "You are a splendid piece of work. You really are. I have heard it said that the Veiled Forge has been looking for you for twenty years, and I confess I thought it an exaggeration." He raises his right hand, palm out, almost gently. "Stand aside."

"No."

The palm descends.

The rod bends.

It does not break. That is the dreadful thing. A bar of black iron as thick as a man's wrist, forged and folded a hundred times, bows in the middle like a bow, and the old refiner goes down on one knee under it, and then on both. The iron screams. A tooth of it flies out of the shaft and spins away across the cobbles. Hu does not let go. He kneels in the gateway with the bent rod over his head and his teeth bared, and the Foundation cultivator looks down at him, with the polite regret of a man who has stepped on something he would rather not have.

"A five-element root," says Zhao Heng, softly. "That is what they call the clever one, I think. The boy in the hut. It's a pity."

His eyes lift, across the yard, across the cobbles, to the narrow slit in the stone wall.

Lin Jian stops breathing.

It is not possible. He is two hundred feet away, in the dark. But the old man's gaze rests on the slit for a long, quiet moment, mild and amused and unhurried, like a man looking at a bird in a cage that he has already decided to buy. Then he smiles, and steps over the kneeling refiner as one steps over a log, and walks on across the yard toward the ring.

* * *

Nine pins burn blue around the hut.

Zhao Heng stops at the edge. He does not touch it. He stands with his head a little on one side, studying the glimmering net, and Lin Jian, who can feel him through the key like a cold hand on the back of the neck, understands why Grandfather said what he said. He will wish to look at it. He does not understand it.

```
[Formation Key :: Ring net]
External pressure: rising
Pins 9 / 12 — load per pin: 41%
Estimated hold time (late FE, direct contact): 14 min
Shell collision at radius 12: ring edge deformation
```

Fourteen minutes.

The Foundation cultivator lays one palm flat against the air.

The ring screams.

It is not a sound. It is a load, a long ragged, tearing strain that runs up the key into the bones of Lin Jian's arm, and the pins go from forty-one to seventy, to ninety, to a hundred, and three of them, on the south side, split their cores with a flat crack and go dark.

```
Pins: 6 of 12
Ring integrity: 52%
Warning: pin 2 critical
```

He bites down on a cry. The hut's stones tremble. The lamp on the floor gutters.

Three in one breath. Fourteen minutes was a lie. He gets his left hand under the right, because the right has begun to shake.

And then, on the other end of the key, down in the dark, he feels something change.

It is a small thing. At first he thinks it is a trick of the strain. The Qi in the plate has been rising steadily since dawn, a long slow climb up a long slow hill. Now it simply stops.

```
Subject: Lin Zhenshan — Stage 2
Compression: 88%
Pulse 71 → 140
Flux through plate: 2.1 → 0.0 → REVERSED
Status: Stage 2 aborted? (unrecognized pattern)
```

Lin Jian stares.

He cannot send the signal. He cannot feel his fingers. Three short, one long. Stay. He has been sending it every five minutes, like a heartbeat, for the last hour, and each time the plate has answered, faintly, like a hand pressed to a hand.

It does not answer now.

Under his feet, in the stone of the hill, a very deep and very old thing begins, slowly, to turn over in its sleep.

The hut trembles. The cicadas, who stopped at dawn, do not start again. Out in the yard, Zhao Heng takes his hand from the air, and for the first time that day his smile is gone.

And the ground begins to shake.
